Key words: insulin resistance, energy expenditure, mitochondria, glucose 
metabolism, hepatic steatosis 
 
 
Abstract: 
Aims: The PDE4 inhibitor roflumilast is a clinically approved anti-inflammatory drug 
used for the treatment of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. In addition, 
roflumilast was found to reduce body weight and improve glucose metabolism by a 
yet unknown mechanism.

Accepted Article
Materials and Methods: Metabolic effects of roflumilast were investigated in 
C57BL/6J mice on high fat western-type diet treated with or without roflumilast for a 
period of 12 weeks.  
Results: Roflumilast led to a marked reduction of body weight gain, which became 
apparent in the second week following treatment initiation and was attributable to a 
pronounced increase of energy expenditure. Furthermore, roflumilast improved 
glucose tolerance, reduced insulin resistance and diminished steatohepatitis of mice. 
Mechanistically, this was associated with hepatic PKA and CREB-activation leading 
to PGC-1α-dependent induction of mitochondrial biogenesis. Consistently, roflumilast 
increased cellular respiratory capacity of hepatocytes in a PKA-dependent manner.  
Conclusion: Roflumilast dependent PDE4-inhibition is a new target for weight loss 
strategies especially in conditions of associated co-morbidities like insulin resistance 
and non-alcoholic steatohepatitis.       
 
Introduction 
An epidemic of obesity is threatening public health at a global level [1]. This is the 
consequence of a sedentary life style affecting large proportions of the population. 
Excessive calorie intake and low energy expenditure lead to inappropriate weight 
gain and accumulation of excessive fat depots. This is followed by a sequeal of 
secondary health problems including type 2 diabetes, non-alcoholic steatohepatitis, 
cardiovascular risk and impairment of the musculoskeletal apparatus as a steadily 
increasing burden for our society [2].

Accepted Article
Treatment strategies focus on life style interventions with the aim to reduce caloric 
intake and augment exercise performance. These recommendations have however 
failed to solve the obesity epidemic, requiring supportive pharmacological or surgical 
interventions. Pharmacological strategies remain challenging due to limited efficacy, 
rebound phenomena and safety limitations [3]. Bariatric surgery has consequently 
proven as the most successful weight loss intervention [4]. Surgical and nutritional 
risks limit this invasive approach, however, to stages of severe obesity. Ongoing 
search aims to identify new drug targets to reduce body weight with acceptable 
efficacy/safety profile and ideally additional beneficial metabolic effects. 
Phosphodiesterases (PDEs) represent a diverse family of phosphodiester 
hydrolyzing enzymes relevant for the metabolism of cyclic nucleotides, which include 
the second messenger cyclic adenosine and guanosine monophosphate (cAMP and 
cGMP) [5]. Both are generated by various G-protein coupled receptors relevant for 
multiple cell communication processes. PDEs can be categorized by structural and 
enzymatic characteristics and substrate specificity to 11 gene family members [5]. 
Among these, the cAMP-metabolizing PDE4 family is comprised of four genes (A-D). 
Alternative splicing of the PDE4 subfamily members gives rise to multiple isoforms. 
All PDE4 subtypes display a related structural organization with a highly conserved 
catalytic domain in the C-terminal region and upstream-conserved regions in the N-
terminal portion of the protein, relevant for protein-interaction and subcellular 
localization [6]. Expression of the PDE4 gene family can ubiquitously be found in all 
tissues with high levels being present in immune regulatory cells [6]. Activation of the 
cAMP pathway in macrophages and granulocytes has potent anti-inflammatory 
actions, which has made PDE4-inhibition an interesting target for inflammatory 
disease processes [7].

Accepted Article
The PDE4 inhibitor roflumilast was specifically developed to treat chronic obstructive 
pulmonary disease (COPD), leading to an effective reduction of COPD 
exacerbations. Roflumilast is highly specific and selective for PDE4 and inhibits 
variants A, B and D with similar efficacy and variant C slightly less efficiently [8]. 
Lower bioavailability and faster plasma clearance of roflumilast in rodents (half-life: 
40 minutes) in comparison to humans (half-life: 11h), requires higher rodent drug 
dosing to achieve comparable plasma levels as reached in humans [9]. 
Interestingly, roflumilast was found to reduce body weight especially in obese 
individuals as well as exerting anti-diabetic effects [6]. The mechanism relevant for 
these metabolic actions remain incompletely understood, prompting us to conduct the 
current investigation.  
 
Material and Methods 
Animal studies 
All experiments were approved by the government of Nordrhein-Westfalen 
(Germany). C57BL/6J mice (n=15 per group) were acquired from Charles River 
Laboratory at the age of 5 weeks and placed in a 12 h day-night cycle with unlimited 
supply of food and water in the animal facility of the University Hospital of the RWTH 
Aachen. After a one week adaptation to our facility, mice were placed on a high fat 
western-type diet (containing 39 kJ% fat, 41 kJ% carbohydrates and 20 kJ% protein 
(ssniff EF R/M acc. TD88137 mod. Western Typ Diet; ssniff Spezialdiäten GmbH) 
supplied with or without roflumilast at a concentration of 21 mg/kg diet. Given the 
accelerated metabolism of roflumilast in rodents this is equivalent to a human daily

Accepted Article
roflumilast dose of 500 µg [10]. Mice were kept on the diet for a period of 12 weeks 
with weekly verification of body weight.  
Intraperitoneal glucose and insulin tolerance tests (ipGTT and ipITT) were conducted 
after 7 and 11 weeks on high fat western-type diet with or without roflumilast. 
Glucose (2 g/kg body weight) or insulin (0.75 U/kg body weight) was injected i.p. after 
a fasting period of 6 h. Blood glucose levels were measured basally and 15, 30, 60, 
90 and 120 minutes after i.p. glucose or insulin injection using a glucometer (Contour, 
Bayer). Glucose-dependent insulin secretion was assessed 10 and 20 minutes after 
glucose injection following the ipGTT protocol.  
At the end of the study, some mice were i.p. injected with insulin (10 U/kg body 
weight) or saline solution. The weight of different tissues was recorded before being 
snap-frozen in liquid nitrogen and stored at -80°C for further analysis.  
Metabolic cages and indirect calorimetric analysis 
Indirect calorimetry was conducted in C57BL/6J male mice on a high fat western-type 
diet with or without roflumilast (n=7 per group) at the animal facility of University of 
Rome "Tor Vergata" in 2014 (January-February). All mice were individually housed 
and acclimatized for 48 h to the metabolic cages. O2 consumption (VO2, ml/h/kg) and 
CO2 production (VCO2, ml/h/kg), food/drink intake and spontaneous locomotor activity 
were measured in mice at 15 min intervals during a 24 h period in the fed state as 
well as during a 12 h period in the fasting state (Labmaster, TSE Systems GmbH, 
Germany). In order to monitor activity an infrared light beam-based locomotion 
monitoring system was used (beam brakes/15min) (n=4 per group). The following 
equations were used for calculation: Respiratory exchange ratio (RER) = [VCO2/VO2]; 
energy expenditure (kcal/h/g) = [(3.815+1.232xRER)xVO2/1000000], as well as using

the Frayn equations (protein oxidation was ignored): glucose oxidation (g/min/kg) = 
[(4.545xVCO2 – 3.205xVO2)/60000] and lipid oxidation (g/min/kg) = [(1.672x(VO2 - 
VCO2))/60000] [11]. Values are corrected according to an effective mass value. All 
studies were performed in accordance to the Guide for the Care and Use of 
Laboratory Animals published by the US National Institutes of Health (NIH 
Publication No. 85e23, revised 1996) and approved by local Institutional Animal 
Committee. 
Blood sample analysis 
Serum concentrations of insulin (Alpco), glucagon (Mercodia) and adiponectin (R&D 
Systems) were determined by enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) 
according to the manufacturer’s protocol. Non-esterified fatty acids (NEFA), 
triglycerides and β-hydroxybutyrate (all Diasys Diagnostics) were measured 
enzymatically by CHOD-PAP method using commercial reagents for photometric 
systems (Tecan). Serum concentration of total glucagon-like peptide 1 (GLP-1) was 
analyzed by using a specific capture antibody (Dianova) against the C-terminus of 
the GLP-1 molecule. A biotinylated secondary antibody against mid-molecular 
epitope (Dianova) was used as detection antibody. Excitation was measured at 450 
nm in a plate reader (Tecan). Circulating liver enzymes like aspartate transaminase 
(AST) and alanine transaminase (ALT) were assessed by the clinical chemistry 
department of the University Hospital Aachen as standard clinical procedure. 
Circulating serum concentrations of interleukin 6 (IL-6), monocyte chemoattractant 
protein 1 (MCP-1) and leptin were detected by Milliplex MAP Kit (Millipore).

Total ribonucleic and deoxyribonucleic acid (RNA and DNA) were isolated with the

followed by DNase digestion and reverse transcription into complementary DNA 
(cDNA) (Invitogen). Gene expression was quantified by use of TaqMan and SYGR 
reagents with a ViiATM 7 Real-Time PCR System (Applied Biosystems).

Oil-Red-O staining 
5 µm liver sections embedded in tissue tek mounting media and fixed in 4 % 
paraformaldehyde were shortly dipped in isopropanol and stained for 15 minutes in a 
0.5 % Oil-Red-O solution. Slices were again dipped in isopropanol, rinsed in tap 
water and finally counterstained with haematoxylin.  
Cell culture and reagents 
Human hepatocellular carcinoma HuH-7 cells (obtained from ThermoFisher 
Scientific) were cultured in Dulbecco's Modified Eagle's Medium (DMEM) (containing 
4.5 g/l glucose) supplemented with 10 % fetal bovine serum (FBS), 1 % penicillin and 
streptomycin at 37 °C and 5 % CO2.

Mouse embryo 3T3-L1 preadipocytes (purchased from American Type Culture 
Collection (ATCC) were cultured in DMEM (containing 4.5 g/l glucose) supplemented 
with 10 % bovine calf serum (BCS; ATCC), 1 % penicillin and streptomycin (P/S) and 
1 mM sodium pyruvate at 37 °C and 5 % CO2. When cells arrived a confluence of 90

for 2 days and then cultured with maintenance medium (DMEM (4.5 g/l glucose) 
containing 10 % FBS, 1 % P/S and 25 IU insulin) until cells were used for the 
experiment. 
For experiments, cells were treated with roflumilast (1 µM, Santa Cruz), PKA 
activator 6-MB-cAMP (100 µM, BioLog), PKA inhibitor 8-Br-cAMPS (1 µM, Enzo) and 
pCPT-cAMP (200 µM, Sigma Aldrich) as a positive control.   
Measurement of Oxygen Consumption Rate (OCR) 
The oxygen consumption rate of HuH-7 and 3T3-L1 cells was assessed by use of 96 
well XF plates (Seahorse Bioscience) at a cell density of 33.000 (HuH-7) and 10.000 
(3T3-L1) cells per well. Cells were treated in cell culture medium with respective 
reagents overnight and equilibrated for 1 h with assay media (DMEM supplemented 
with 4.5 g/l glucose, 2 mM sodium pyruvate and 2 mM glutamine). The experimental 
protocol followed the company’s suggestions with each cycle compromising 3 
repeats of 3 minutes mixing and 3 minutes measuring procedure. OCR was 
assessed basally and after addition of oligomycin at a final concentration of 1 µM 
(Huh-7) and 1.5 µM (3T3-L1), then FCCP (0.4 µM (Huh-7) and 0.75 µM (3T3-L1)) 
and finally a combination of antimycin A and rotenone (each 1 µM for both cell types). 
All measurements were normalized to protein content.

Active PKA assay 
Liver tissue was homogenized using western blot lysis buffer and PKA activity 
determined by use of “PKA kinase activity kit” (Enzo) normalized to total protein 
concentration.  
Flow cytometry 
Liver tissue was digested in a 2 % collagenase IV (Cell Systems) solution fallowed by 
a step to lysate the erythrocytes (BD Biosciences). Samples were then stacked to a 
lymphocyte separation media (LSM 1077; PAA) to perform a density gradient 
centrifugation. Cells were stained with the fallowing antibodies: CD45, Ly6G, Ly6G 
and Ly6C (all acquired from BD Biosciences), F4/80 (Serotec) and CD11b 
(eBioscience). Dead cells were excluded by Hoechst 33258 dye (BD Biosciences). 
Flow-cytometric analysis was performed on a FACS-Canto II running FACS Diva 7.0 
(BD Biosciences) and analysed with FlowJo (Tree Star). 
Statistical analysis 
Data are presented as the mean ± standard error of the mean (SEM) performed by 
GraphPad Prism 6.0 (GraphPad Software Inc.). Analysis of the data was compared 
using unpaired or multiple t-test or by one- or two-way ANOVA were indicated and 
statistical significance was assigned at p<0.05.  
 
Results 
Roflumilast reduces body weight and increases energy expenditure 
To evaluate the metabolic effects of roflumilast-dependent PDE4-inhibition we treated 
C57BL/6J mice on high fat western-type diet with or without roflumilast (21 mg/kg

--- Page 11 ---

Accepted Article
diet; which results in equivalent roflumilast plasma concentrations as found in 
humans with the clinically approved dose of 500 µg/day) for a period of 12 weeks [9]. 
Similar expression levels of the PDE4 variants A, B and D were found in muscle and 
brown adipose tissue of roflumilast treated and control animals, while PDE4C mRNA 
expression was not detectable (supplementary figure 1a and b). A significant 
increase of PDE4B mRNA expression was found in white adipose tissue with a non-
significant trend in liver tissue of roflumilast treated animals (supplementary figure 1c 
and d), which was however not confirmed by protein level (supplementary figure 1e, f 
and g). 
Roflumilast let to an early reduction of body weight gain relative to control animals, 
which became apparent in the second week following treatment initiation (figure 1a) 
and remained significant until the end of the study period. This was accompanied by 
a significant reduction of liver- and epididymal adipose tissue weight at necropsy 
(figures 1b) in addition to decreased circulating leptin levels (figure 1d). 
Mechanistically, body weight reduction was associated with a significant induction of 
energy expenditure by roflumilast, detectable during the dark period (figure 1c and 
table 1), which was primarily driven by increased glucose oxidation (figure 1e and 
table 1). Paradoxically this was accompanied by a significant increase of food 
consumption of roflumilast treated animals during the dark period (table 1), while no 
difference was detected for physical activity between groups (supplement figure 2a 
and table 1). 
Roflumilast improves glucose tolerance and insulin sensitivity 
In addition to the reduction of body weight gain we found roflumilast treatment to 
significantly lower fasting glucose levels. In addition, roflumilast significantly 
decreased circulating MCP-1 concentrations, while leaving circulating levels of free

Accepted Article
fatty acids, triglyceride, β-hydroxybuturate, total GLP-1, glucagon, adiponectin and 
IL-6 unaffected (table 2). This was accompanied by a significant improvement of 
glucose tolerance (figure 1f) and insulin sensitivity (figure 1g) of roflumilast-treated 
animals, also leading to reduced glucose-dependent insulin secretion (figure 1h). 
Consistently we found insulin-signaling to be significantly improved in liver and white 
adipose tissue - as detected by Akt-phosphorylation - of roflumilast-treated animals 
(figure 1i-k). No difference of pancreatic islet size was detected between groups (data 
not shown).  
We next asked whether improved hepatic insulin sensitivity was associated with a 
reduction of hepatic steatosis. Indeed, hepatic lipid content was profoundly 
decreased in roflumilast treated animals (figure 1l) featuring significantly lower levels 
of hepatic cholesterol and triglyceride content (figure 1m). In addition, we found 
circulating liver enzyme levels to be decreased by roflumilast, suggesting improved 
steatohepatitis (figure 1n). This was confirmed by reduced hepatic expression of the 
macrophage marker F4/80 in addition to reduced expression of the inflammatory 
marker serum amyloid A (figure 1o). Exploratory FACS analysis further suggested 
reduced hepatic infiltration by inflammatory Ly-6Chigh macrophages in roflumilast 
treated animals, while simultaneously a lower number of anti-inflammatory Ly-6Clow 
macrophages were found after treatment with the PDE4 inhibitor (figure 1p). In 
addition, we found hepatic collagen expression as an indicator of fibrogenesis to be 
significantly reduced in roflumilast-treated animals (figure 1o).  
Roflumilast up-regulates mitochondrial function in hepatocytes 
To elucidate the relevant mechanisms for roflumilast-induced metabolic effects, we 
assessed hepatic PKA-activity as an effector target of the second messenger cAMP, 
which we found to be significantly increased by roflumilast (figure 2a). Furthermore,

CREB-phosphorylation - a downstream target of PKA actions - was significantly 
increased in liver tissue of roflumilast treated animals (figure 2b) together with 
enhanced AMPK and p38 MAPK phosphorylation (figures 2c and 2d). As these 
signaling pathways mimicked the hepatic response to glucagon, we next assessed 
the hepatic expression of peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor gamma 
coactivator 1-alpha (PGC-1α) and phosphoenolpyruvate carboxykinase-1 (PEPCK) 
as downstream glucagon targets (figure 2e), which we also found to be significantly 
increased by roflumilast. In contrast, hepatic expression of glucose 6-phosphate 
(G6P), which is relevant to mediate the final step of gluconeogenesis, was 
significantly reduced by roflumilast treatment (figure 2e). In addition, activation of the 
FoxO transcription factors - as main positive regulators of gluconeogenesis and direct 
downstream targets of Akt - were significantly reduced by roflumilast (figures 2f and 
2g). This mechanism may contribute to improved insulin sensitivity of roflumilast 
treated animals with Akt-dependent FoxO-phosphorylation mediating its nuclear 
export and degradation [12]. 
As PGC-1α is known to increase mitochondrial biogenesis, we next assessed hepatic 
mitochondrial DNA content (figure 2h), which together with the mitochondrial 
transcription factor A (Tfam) and nuclear respiratory factor 1 (Nrf-1) were significantly 
increased by roflumilast (figure 2i). Furthermore, genes relevant for mitochondrial 
fusion (mitofusin 1 (Mfn-1), mitofusin 2 (Mfn-2), by trend Optic atrophy 1 (Opa1) and 
fission (Dynamin-1-like protein (Drp-1), mitochondrial fission 1 protein (Fis-1)) were 
significantly up-regulated in the liver of roflumilast treated animals (figure 2j). A 
similar induction of mitochondrial genes was found in white adipose tissue (figures 2k 
and 2l) but not in muscle tissue (supplementary figure 2b) of respective animals. In 
addition, no relevant difference of uncoupling protein expression (UCP-1/2/3) was 
found in liver or in the white/brown adipose tissue depots investigated in this study

(supplementary figure 2c-e). We next asked whether PDE4-inhibition would stimulate 
the cellular respiratory capacity of hepatocytes or adipocytes. Roflumilast increased 
cellular respiratory capacity of human hepatocellular carcinoma HuH7 cells in a 
comparable manner as found in response to cAMP (figures 3a and b) but not in 
differentiated mouse 3T3-L1 adipocytes (supplementary figure 2f). As cAMP is known 
to signal in a PKA-dependent manner, we next used the specific PKA activator (6-
MB-cAMP), which similarly increased respiratory capacity of hepatocytes, while PKA-
inhibition abolished roflumilast-dependent induction of respiratory capacity (figure 3c 
to 3f). This demonstrates roflumilast-induced PKA activation to be necessary and 
sufficient for the increase of the hepatocyte respiratory capacity by the treatment, 
which might hold relevance for the observed induction of energy expenditure, weight 
loss and reduced steatosis of roflumilast treated animals.    
 
Discussion 
This study addressed the metabolic consequences of roflumilast dependent PDE4-
inhibition and the underlying molecular mechanisms in a mouse model of metabolic 
syndrome. Others have recently reported PDE4 expression to be increased by high 
fat western-type diet in mice [13]. We found roflumilast to reduce body weight of 
western-type diet fed mice. This was mediated by an increase of energy expenditure, 
which caused sufficient caloric loss of roflumilast-treated animals despite a 
paradoxical increase of food intake, while no change of locomotor activity was 
recorded. Increased food intake of roflumilast treated animals most likely represents 
a compensatory response to the increase of energy expenditure, potentially mediated 
by the observed reduction of leptin levels, which requires further investigations [14].

Accepted Article
A similar weight phenotype has been reported for PDE4B knockout mice, which was 
however attributed to increased locomotor activity, while no difference in energy 
expenditure was recorded [15]. Roflumilast dependent energy expenditure therefore 
seems unlikely to be mediated by PDE4B inhibition. Alternatively, differences in the 
background strain of mice (which was 25% 129/Ola and 75% C57BL/6 in the study of 
Zhang et al.) might be relevant for the seemingly contradicting results [15]. 
Interestingly we found roflumilast treatment to significantly increase white adipose 
tissue PDE4B mRNA expression, which was however not confirmed for protein . 
Additional experiments, using specific knockout models for the different PDE4 genes 
- preferentially in combination with roflumilast treatment - will be required to identify 
the relevant PDE4 family member. 
Importantly, roflumilast was also found to reduce body weight in humans [16, 17]. 
This became apparent in COPD treatment trials, in which weight loss constitutes a 
potential safety limitation. Interestingly, body weight loss was more pronounced in 
obese than lean individuals [16, 17]. However, only two studies specifically 
addressed the body weight reducing potential of roflumilast in humans, which were 
performed in women with polycystic ovarian (PCO) syndrome. Combined treatment 
of roflumilast with metformin reduced body weight by 4.2 kg while a metformin-
monotherapy only led to a 0.9 kg body weight reduction during a 12 week trial, which 
was mainly attributable to reduced fat mass [18]. In the second study, roflumilast 
reduced body weight more efficiently than metformin but less pronounced than 
liraglutide during a 12 week trial [19]. Whether an increase of energy expenditure 
contributes to the weight loss potential of roflumilast in humans is currently unknown 
and will require further investigations.

On the molecular level roflumilast-dependent PDE4-inhibition increased hepatic PKA 
activity followed by CREB-phosphorylation and increased expression of PGC-1α (as 
schematically illustrated in figure 3g). PGC-1α serves as a master regulator of 
mitochondrial biogenesis by co-activation of various transcription factors including 
peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor (PPARs), estrogen-related receptors 
(ERR), nuclear respiratory factors (Nrf-1 and Nrf-2) and mitochondrial transcription 
factor A (Tfam) [20-22]. Consistently, we found mitochondrial DNA content to be 
increased in liver tissue of roflumilast-treated animals in vivo, while in-vitro roflumilast 
dependent PDE4-inhibition augmented the respiratory capacity of hepatocytes in a 
PKA-dependent manner. A similar induction of mitochondrial factors was observed in 
adipose tissue, which suggests a comparable effect of PDE4-inhibition in different 
tissues. This stimulation of mitochondrial biogenesis and respiratory capacity is likely 
to be responsible for increased energy expenditure of roflumilast-treated animals, 
which warrants further investigations.  
Importantly, we found roflumilast to markedly improve glucose metabolism, which 
was mediated by improved insulin sensitivity and illustrated by increased Akt 
phosphorylation in different tissues. This can at least partially be attributed to the 
observed weight loss phenotype of roflumilast-treated animals, as reduction of lipid 
accumulation and lipotoxicity solves a major cause for insulin resistance in 
metabolically relevant tissues [23]. Consistent with our results others have found 
roflumilast treatment to improve glucose metabolism in db/db mice. Importantly, this 
was found is the absence of body weight reduction and attributed to an induction of 
GLP-1 mediated insulin secretion [24]. In contrast, no difference of total GLP-1 levels 
was found in our model, while roflumilast significantly increased insulin sensitivity and 
food consumption. These seemingly conflicting data might be due to differential 
genetic backgrounds of applied mouse models. As a relevant limitation our study did

not include a normal chow and weight maintained (roflumilast matched) high fat 
western-type diet control groups. We are consequently unable to discriminate 
whether roflumilast holds additional, body weight-independent effects on glucose 
metabolism. Others have found caloric restriction and weight loss to be sufficient for 
AMPK-activation leading to increased PGC-1α activation, which was similarly 
associated to improved glucose metabolism as found in our study [25-28]. Additional 
experiments including the above mentioned control groups will be required to 
characterize direct effects of roflumilast on glucose metabolism. These effects might 
be mediated by the immune-modulatory/anti-inflammatory capacities of roflumilast, 
which would similarly be expected to improve insulin sensitivity [29]. Importantly 
roflumilast was also found to improve glucose metabolism in humans, leading to a 
mean HbA1c-reduction of 0.45% in patients with newly diagnosed diabetes during a 
12 week randomized trial [30].  
On a molecular level we found roflumilast treatment to partially mimic the hepatic 
response to glucagon. Activation of the glucagon receptor causes Gs protein-
dependent stimulation of adenylate cyclase activity with consecutive increase of 
cAMP, leading to PKA and CREB activation and induction of gluconeogenesis gene

increased PEPCK expression - as a CREB target gene - in our model, which 
catalyzes the primary step of gluconeogenesis [35]. In contrast, roflumilast 
suppressed G6P expression - which catalyzes the terminal step of gluconeogenesis 
[35]. This illustrates an unexpected and opposing regulation of the two main

found hepatic FoxO-activation as a main regulator of gluconeogenesis to be

have reported FoxO signaling to have higher relevance for G6P than PEPCK

impaired cAMP responsiveness of G6P but not PEPCK [39]. This observation 
suggests chronic PDE4-inhibition to separate cAMP-dependent stimulation of 
mitochondrial biogenesis from hepatic gluconeogenesis, which makes PDE4-
inhibition an attractive target for pharmacological weight loss interventions. Indeed, 
recent investigations also suggest glucagon receptor activation to potently reduce 
body weight when applied in combination with GLP-1 receptor activation [40]. 
Importantly, this similarly improved insulin sensitivity as found in our model [41].  
Finally and consistent with other studies we found roflumilast-dependent PDE4-
inhibition to improve steatohepatitis [6]. This might be the consequence of reduced 
hepatic lipid content and/or reflect anti-inflammatory, immune-modulatory efficacy of 
the drug, which requires further investigations.

roflumilast and are consequently unable to demonstrate equivalent circulating drug 
concentrations as found in humans treated with the recommended daily dose of 500 
µg.
